sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies. I assumed this is the pricing page of a SaaS scheduling and booking tool, where visitors compare three plans and pick one. The image is 1280×800, about one screen, so I worked from the whole image without crops.

**Findings**
None of the checklist lines got a `no`. The copy has three problems that no checklist line covers. The director decides how to file them:

1. **The prices can be read two ways.** This is at "$9 / month", "$29 / month" and "$79 / month" (y≈405, cards at x≈190, 519 and 847). The Team and Business plans are sold to groups, so "$29 / month" could mean a flat price for the team or $29 for each person. A buyer who assumes a flat price and later gets a bill per person will feel misled, and price is what they hold you to. Fix: say the unit ("per team" or "per user") next to each price. **Defect. Major.**
2. **The feature lists don't say whether higher plans include the lower ones.** This is in the three lists at y≈465–525. Business lists "Unlimited calendars, Single sign-on, Priority support" but doesn't mention Booking page, Email reminders, Shared availability or Reports. A stranger can't tell whether the $79 plan loses the features of the cheaper plans. Buyers usually assume each tier includes the one below, but the page never says so, and the purchase depends on it. Fix: start each higher plan's list with "Everything in Team, plus:" (or the matching lower plan). **Defect. Major.**
3. **The subhead is generic and partly contradicts the page.** This is "Simple plans for teams of every size. Change or cancel whenever you like." at y≈221–248. The first sentence could sit on any SaaS pricing page, and "teams" doesn't fit the Solo plan. The second sentence is the useful promise, but it is set as an afterthought. Fix: lead with what is specific, such as the cancellation terms or a free trial if there is one. That second option ties in with "Start free" at top right (x≈1107–1215, y≈14–56), which hints at a free trial that the pricing area never mentions. **Taste. Minor.** (Whether each plan card needs its own button is a question for the interface and arrangement critics, not this one.)

**What's working.**
- Type, colour and shape share one calm style: a single blue accent, pale grey card borders and one sans-serif family. The page reads as one product, not a collage.
- The three cards repeat exactly the same structure (name, price, three features) at the same positions. You can compare across the row without searching.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 8 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure.

sections.report:
**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Below the first element, can you tell each level of the text (title, headings, body, captions) from the next at a glance, with no two sizes almost the same?** No. The three prices ($9, $29, $79 at about 190–930 × 385–425) look nearly as tall as the "Pricing" title (about 565–715 × 140–185), and both are bold and set in the same dark navy. The title is only slightly larger than the prices, so the eye can't tell which one outranks the other. It treats them as one level and goes back and forth between a word that tells it nothing (the nav already shows "Pricing" as the current page) and the numbers it came for.
   - **Why:** a difference that is meant to be there should be obvious at a glance, and a one-step difference looks like an accident (Dair, *Design with Type*, ch. 8). Sizes should come from a small scale where each size is its own level (Bringhurst, *The Elements of Typographic Style*, 3.1.1).
   - **The small sizes collide too:** feature lines (about 15 px), "/ month" and the nav links (about 16 px), and the subtitle (about 18 px) are only a pixel or two apart. That points to sizes picked one at a time. It doesn't hurt much here, because colour and position keep their jobs apart.
   - **Fix:** separate the title and the prices clearly. On a pricing page the prices are the content, so either make the title smaller (or turn it into a heading that says something about the offer) or make the prices clearly the largest type on the page. Then merge the 15–18 px sizes into one body size and one detail size.
   - **Type and weight:** defect for the title/price collision (major), convention for the small-size drift (minor).

2. **Not a checklist line, from the first read: the cards have no hierarchy, so nothing tells you which plan to pick.** The three cards (162–461, 490–789 and 818–1117 × 306–570) are identical in size, border, weight and colour. None is marked as recommended, and none has its own button. The only call to action is "Start free" up in the nav (1107–1216 × 14–57), well away from the prices. A visitor comparing plans scans three equal boxes, gets no hint about which one fits a team, and has to find their way back up to the nav to act. That's usually where a pricing page loses people.
   - **Fix:** give one plan (most likely Team) a clear visual lead through a tinted or heavier card, a label, or a filled button, and put an ask on each card, close to its price.
   - **Type and weight:** taste on which plan to highlight, defect on the missing per-card action. Major.

**What's working.**
- Plan names are bold and dark, while feature lines are regular weight in a lighter grey-blue. Each card reads as name, price, details because of weight and colour, not size alone.
- The title block is centred with lots of space around it, so the eye lands right away and knows where to start. There's no competing focal point above the cards.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** I couldn't run the crop and entries scripts because Bash was denied in this session. All sizes above are eyeballed from the full 1280×800 image. To confirm finding 1, measure the "Pricing" title against the price numbers.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 2 yes, 1 no (each text level distinct, no two sizes almost the same)

sections.report:
**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does the arrangement lead the eye from the first element through the rest, with no line, gaze, or pointing shape that leads it off the edge?** The eye moves cleanly from "Pricing" (y≈160) to the subtitle and then into the three cards. It ends at the last feature line of each card (y≈525), and nothing comes after that. The only action on the page is "Start free" in the top-right corner (x≈1107–1216, y≈14–57), about 500 px up and to the right of where the eye stops. A viewer who has just picked a plan has to leave the card and go hunting for what to do next. Nothing on the page connects a chosen tier to that button either, so the choice the cards ask for has no step after it. Direction: give the path a destination where it ends. Put an action at the foot of each card, in the empty band that is already there at y≈540–570, so the eye goes plan → features → act without backtracking. The hierarchy and interface critics may raise the missing per-card action as well; here the point is that the arrangement dead-ends. **Defect.** Weight: **major**.
2. **Do all blocks, pictures included, take their edges and the gaps between them from one grid, so column lines and gutters repeat down the page?** The page uses two unrelated containers. The header runs from x≈64 (logo) to x≈1216 (button edge). The content runs from x≈162 to x≈1118 (outer card edges). The nav links start at x≈223, which lines up with nothing below. No edge in the header continues down into the content, so the top bar and the body look like two separate layouts stacked together rather than one page. Inside the content area the grid is sound: three ≈300 px cards with equal ≈28 px gutters. Direction: make the content column share the header's edges, or make the header's inner edges land on the card column lines (for example, the nav starting at the card column's left edge). **Convention.** Weight: **minor**.

**What's working.**
- The three cards are exactly the same width, with equal gutters, centered on the same axis as the heading (x≈640). Inside each card the name, price and feature list sit at the same heights, so prices and features line up across the row and can be compared side by side without the eye hunting.
- Space clearly separates the groups. The gaps inside a card (≈30 px between feature lines) are smaller than the gaps between name, price and features (≈40–45 px), and those are smaller than the gap between the header block and the cards. Each card reads as one unit with three clear parts.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Below the cards, the band from y≈570 to 800 is empty. I can't tell whether this is the end of the page or more content (an FAQ, a comparison table) just below the fold. If the page really ends there, the pricing section stops abruptly and finding 1 gets worse. Check this in a live browser.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 11 yes, 2 no (one grid governs the page; clear eye path)

Note: the crop and entries scripts couldn't be run because Bash was refused in this session. I judged the image whole, which works at this size (about one screen), and answered both `no` lines from the checklist wording without opening their reference entries.

sections.report:
I'm doing the deep read now. The text section comes out mostly clean, with one real finding. The report follows.

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do paragraphs and columns break cleanly, with no lone short word on a last line and no heading at the foot of a column?** The two-line subtitle under "Pricing" (about x 360–920, y 210–260) wraps so that its second line is just "you like." (x≈605–675, y≈248). The first line is about 70 characters and the second is two words. The intro ends on a stub that looks like a mistake, and the centred block reads lopsided right under the page's strongest heading. Bringhurst (*The Elements of Typographic Style*, 2.4.2) says not to leave a short word alone on a last line. Fix: balance the two lines, either by narrowing the text box or with `text-wrap: balance`, so each line holds about half the sentence. Or cut the copy to fit on one line. **Convention.** Weight: **minor**.

**What's working.**
- **Clear type steps.** One sans family carries the whole page in clearly separate sizes: heading, prices, plan names, then list and nav text. Weight and grey do the fine work instead of extra sizes, so every level has an obvious job (Refactoring UI: bolder, not bigger).
- **Prices you can't misread.** Each price is set large and bold, with "/ month" small and grey right next to it. The number reads first and the unit is still attached to it, so you can't read the price two ways.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether the subtitle's "you like." stub is fixed in the build or only shows at this window width. Check the wrap at a few widths in a live browser.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 29 yes, 1 no (paragraphs break cleanly, with no runt), 0 unsure

First read: the eye lands on the "Pricing" heading, then moves across three identical white cards. The blue "Tidewell" logo at top left and the blue "Start free" button at top right frame the header. It reads as a clean, plain SaaS pricing page and feels calm. It also looks templated.

Job (assumed): a SaaS pricing page that helps small-team buyers compare plans and start a trial.

Walk (Color):
- Small palette: yes. White, a few cool grays, navy-black text and one blue.
- Saturated color kept to a small share: yes. Blue appears only in the logo and the button.
- Clear value range: yes. Dark navy type on white; the pale card borders still read in grayscale.
- Warm forward, cool recede: yes. No warm colors, and nothing needs to come forward except the button, which saturation already handles.
- Matching colors look the same: yes. The logo blue and the button blue match.
- No vibrating edges: yes.
- Status colors used for their usual meaning: yes. Blue is used as the brand and action color.
- Meaning not carried by color alone: yes. Nothing on the page carries meaning through color.
- Dark theme background: yes. This is a light theme, so the line doesn't apply.

No line answered no or unsure, so I opened no entries.

**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **Restrained palette.** The page uses one blue on a white and cool-gray base. The blue appears only on the logo (about x 64–155, y 24–48) and the "Start free" button (x 1107–1216, y 14–57). Because it is the only saturated area, the button is the one obvious action on the page (Refactoring UI; Albers on how a color reads against its surroundings). Keep the blue for actions only. If a "recommended" plan or per-card buttons are added, take them from the same blue rather than adding a second hue.
- **Value carries the structure.** Plan names and prices are dark navy-black. Prices like "$29" are near-black, while "/ month" and the feature lists are a lighter slate gray. That puts the price on a step above its details through lightness, without needing another size or color. The page still reads correctly in grayscale.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

sections.report:
**Walk (working notes)**

The image is 1280×800, one screen, so I worked from the whole image. Bash is denied, so I couldn't run the crop or entries scripts.

First read: the eye lands on the "Pricing" heading, then moves across the three large prices. The blue "Start free" button at top right pulls next. It reads as a SaaS pricing page for a scheduling or booking tool. It is clean and generic. Assumed job: get a visitor to pick a plan and start.

Interface:
- One primary button: yes. "Start free" is the only filled button.
- Controls look like what they do: yes. Nav links follow the usual top-nav convention.
- Non-text contrast 3:1: yes. The card borders are pale, but they are decorative containers, not control edges.
- States shown distinct: yes. No states are shown.
- Focus indicator: unsure. No focus is shown.
- Focus not obscured: unsure. I can't tell whether the header is sticky.
- Main content uncovered: yes.
- Target size: yes. "Start free" is about 109×43; nav links are well spaced.
- Phone thumb zone: yes (not a phone layout).
- Shows where the user is: **no**. "Pricing" in the nav looks the same as the other items.
- Way out: yes (no dialog).
- Inputs: yes (none).
- Destructive actions: yes (none).
- Recognition over recall: **no**. Each card lists different features, so you can't tell whether Team has email reminders or Business has reports.
- Progressive disclosure: yes.
- Form lines and errors: yes (none).
- Empty state: yes (none).
- Help near a complex step: yes.
- Shortcuts: yes (not relevant on a marketing page).
- Anticipation: **no**. There is no action in any card, and the only "Start free" button is far away and names no plan.
- Conventions: yes.
- Audience's words: **no**. "calendars" is the product's unit, not the buyer's, and "/ month" doesn't say whether it is per seat.
- Link purpose: yes.
- Sensory instructions: yes.
- Conceptual model: **no**. "Product" and "Features" overlap.
- Consistency across screens: yes (one screen).
- Reflow: yes.
- Dark patterns: yes.

---

**Section.** Interface: applies (top nav, "Start free" button, plan cards that should lead to an action).

**Findings**
1. **Does the screen put what the user likely needs next in front of them (the next action)?**
   - **Where:** the three plan cards (x 162–1117, y 306–569) end after their feature lists. None has a button or link. The only action on the page is "Start free" at top right (≈1107–1216, 14–57), about 300 px above the cards and 400–900 px across from them.
   - **What the viewer meets:** someone who has just decided on "Team" has nothing to press there. They have to travel back to the header and press a button that doesn't say which plan it starts, or whether "free" means a trial of Team or a free Solo plan. The moment of decision on a pricing page is lost.
   - **Why:** this is common sense here. The catalog's anticipation entry (Tognazzini) is off the reading list, so I don't cite it. It also matches pricing-page convention.
   - **Fix:** put one action at the foot of each card that names the plan and what happens ("Start Team free for 14 days" or similar). Keep the header button as the general entry.
   - **Kind:** defect. **Weight:** major.

2. **Is everything the user needs to act visible on this screen, with nothing to remember from another?**
   - **Where:** the feature lists (y ≈ 465–525). Each card names three different features, and no card says "everything in Solo, plus".
   - **What the viewer meets:** the viewer can't tell whether Team includes the booking page and email reminders, or whether Business includes shared availability and reports. To compare, they have to guess, or hold one card in mind while reading the next.
   - **Why:** Nielsen heuristic 6, recognition rather than recall.
   - **Fix:** either add "Everything in Solo, plus:" to Team and "Everything in Team, plus:" to Business, or use shared rows with ticks.
   - **Kind:** defect. **Weight:** major. It decides whether the viewer can choose a plan at all.

3. **Do labels and messages use the audience's own words rather than internal or system terms?**
   - **Where:** "1 calendar", "Up to 10 calendars" and "Unlimited calendars" in the first feature line, and "/ month" beside every price.
   - **What the viewer meets:** a team lead thinks in people. "10 calendars" could mean 10 team members or 10 connected calendars, and so could "1 calendar" on a plan called Solo. "$29 / month" reads two ways: $29 flat for the team, or $29 per user. The wrong reading changes the real bill by up to 10×. This is a price line, so the viewer will hold the company to it.
   - **Why:** Nielsen heuristic 2, match between system and the real world. It is also a price whose meaning is ambiguous.
   - **Fix:** say the unit the buyer pays by ("up to 10 team members"), and state "per month, billed for the whole team" or "per user per month" next to the price.
   - **Kind:** defect. **Weight:** major.

4. **Does the screen show where the user is, such as the current page?**
   - **Where:** "Pricing" in the nav (≈436–488, y 36) has the same grey and weight as Product, Features, Customers and Contact.
   - **What the viewer meets:** the page heading says Pricing, so the loss is small. But the nav gives no "you are here", and a visitor arriving from search gets no confirmation of where Pricing sits in the site.
   - **Why:** Nielsen heuristic 1, visibility of system status.
   - **Fix:** mark the current item with weight, colour or an underline. Colour alone would also need a second cue.
   - **Kind:** convention. **Weight:** minor.

5. **Do the grouping, names, and navigation show how the product's parts relate?**
   - **Where:** the nav items "Product" and "Features" sit side by side (≈223–391, y 36).
   - **What the viewer meets:** two labels for what is usually the same thing. The viewer can't predict which one holds what, and may open both.
   - **Why:** Norman, conceptual model. This is my judgment of these two labels, not a measured fact.
   - **Fix:** merge them, or rename one so its content is clear (for example "How it works" vs "Integrations").
   - **Kind:** taste. **Weight:** minor.

**What's working.**
- There is one unmistakable primary button. "Start free" is the only filled, saturated control on the page, so nothing competes with it for "what do I press". Keep that single primary when you add per-card actions: style those lower, or make only the recommended plan's button filled.
- The nav is a plain, conventional top bar: logo left, five text links, action right. A visitor finds it without thinking.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Focus indicators on the nav links and "Start free". Check that each has a visible ring at least 2 px thick with 3:1 contrast.
- Whether the header is sticky and would cover focused controls or the cards when scrolling.
- Whether the cards are clickable as a whole. If they are, nothing signals it.

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 26 yes, 5 no (current page shown; recognition rather than recall; next action in front of the user; audience's own words; conceptual model), 2 unsure (focus indicator; focus not obscured)

Note: Bash was denied, so I couldn't run the crop or entries scripts. I read the 1280×800 image whole and argued the findings from the named heuristics without opening the catalog entries.
